newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon halts special media permit for Hizbollah.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon halts special media permit for Hizbollah.

text.p: Lebanon clamped down further on media outlets on Wednesday, cancelling a permit to Hizbollah television and radio stations to broadcast news of guerrilla warfare in south Lebanon.

The Lebanese cabinet announced the decision as dozens of private television and radio stations refrained from broadcasting news bulletins and political programmes a day after the government refused to license them.

The government ban -- and its order for most of them to close by the end of November -- caused a storm of protest among opposition politicians who said it was an attempt to curb press freedoms and to allow political chiefs to monopolise the media.
The government licensed only 15 television and radio stations on Tuesday out of nearly 200 media outlets dominating air waves since the 1975-1990 civil war.

It originally permitted Hizbollah's al-Manar television and al-Nour radio to operate "as long as Israel occupied Lebanese land" although the stations did not get a license. The pro-Iranian Hizbollah is fighting to push Israel out of a self-declared security zone in southern Lebanon.
The reversal comes just after parliamentary elections, when tense relations between Sunni Moslem billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri and Hizbollah degenerated into a war of words.
Hariri has openly said that the elections were a clash between "extremists" and "moderates".

Announcing the reversal of this exception, Information Minister Farid Makari said after a cabinet session on Wednesday the government confirmed the licensing of four television stations and 11 radio stations owned by political leaders or businessmen but without "making any exception to any party".

Al-Nour radio did not broadcast a scheduled daily news bulletin after Makari announced the decision. Hizbollah (Party of God) officials were not available for comment but the group had on Tuesday attacked the government decision.

"The cabinet decision is a political one aiming at silencing the voice of the opposition through licensing television and radio stations which it can control," the militant group said in a statement issued in Beirut newspapers.

A follow-up committee grouping media proprietors said in a statement on Wednesday: "This decision to divide the media among a number of top political officials goes beyound authority limits and is against the constitution and the basic rules of democracy".
The government left the door open for granting more licenses if stations refiled applications to a government-appointed agency to restudy their situations by the end of November.

The government licensed the following television stations: Future Television of Hariri, NBN, a station which Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri is reported to be setting up, MTV of the brother of Deputy Prime Minister Michel al-Murr and Lebanon's top private station LBCI.
It also licensed a radio station owned by Hariri, another one Berri is setting up, and a third owned by local investors.
